cells.quote: "Five of the 15 educators we interviewed described the difficulty of establishing new QISE courses, especially securing regular approvals to offer these courses."
cells.note: Quote is from the wiki entry; the supplied study-text excerpt does not include this sentence. The interview study reports a challenge, but does not specify a comparison condition or quantify an effect.

O.outcome_detail: bureaucratic and administrative difficulty obtaining program approvals

cells.quote:
Program-level Goals findings from the same interview corpus. The article states this program-level weakness was "an expanded version of the administrative challenge of setting up a QISE course", with approvals through deans and faculty senate.

"Five participants echoed similar challenges, which underscores the bureaucratic processes that complicate the creation of new programs."
cells.note: The supplied study text does not include the reported program-level findings verbatim; the quote is copied from the wiki entry. The qualitative contrast indicates greater administrative difficulty for programs than courses.

D.treatment: Explicitly clarify challenging QIST concepts and misinformation

cells.quote: Educators interviewed highlighted the need to carefully address aspects of QIST concepts that might be confusing or could contribute to misinformation. To counter misinformation, he suggested that “one has to emphasize that whatever else you may think about how the universe works, it doesn't allow us to send signals faster than light”.
cells.note: Interview-based educator recommendation; no comparative learning outcome was measured.

D.treatment: Use vetted videos, simulations, articles, and expert public communication
D.comparison: Unvetted online resources and misleading media coverage

cells.quote: Educators sharing with their students at all levels vetted resources on the internet, e.g., videos, simulations, articles and other tools, so that they can learn from them as self-paced learning tools or as part of a course in which the educators and students will also discuss those ideas in class
cells.note: The study reports educators’ suggestions rather than a tested comparison or effect.

D.treatment: Compare misleading and accurate QIST articles or videos in class discussion
D.comparison: Reading or watching sources without comparative analysis

cells.quote: Then there can be class discussions comparing the content of both types of articles and why it is important to go beyond the flashy headlines to understand these fascinating QIST concepts.
cells.note: This is a proposed classroom activity; the article does not report an evaluation of its effectiveness.

D.treatment: Hands-on, kinesthetic, and game-based activities for quantum concepts
D.comparison: Classical situation or less active learning approaches

cells.quote: These games give students opportunities to collect and analyze data and understand how these observations are different from what they would observe in a classical situation. These games make it easier for students to have a good mental model of quantum concepts in a motivating and engaging environment.
cells.note: The positive claim summarizes cited game-based studies, but this article does not provide a new quantitative comparison or effect size.

O.outcome_detail: depth and specialization of required quantum knowledge

cells.quote: As the level of quantum expertise increases to quantum proficient and quantum expert, so does the degree of specialization of the roles.
cells.note: This is an observational comparison of job-role requirements, not an instructional treatment comparison.

O.outcome_detail: required quantum expertise and quantum-specific KSAs

cells.quote: For roles requiring quantum expertise, we describe the quantum KSAs required. For the roles that do not involve any quantum-specific expertise, we instead summarize their primary responsibilities and explain their importance within QISE companies.
cells.note: The contrast concerns occupational requirements; the study does not measure learning or performance outcomes.

O.outcome_detail: quantum knowledge-and-skill profile required for tasks

cells.quote: The first category of tasks involves primarily hands-on experimental work. These tasks require advanced lab skills relevant to quantum systems, along with an understanding of the underlying theoretical concepts.\n\nThe final category of tasks require only theoretical knowledge of quantum or QISE.
cells.note: The text reports different KSA profiles across task types, not a better-than comparison or an instructional intervention.

D.treatment: Connect instruction to learners’ prior knowledge while avoiding oversimplification
D.comparison: Oversimplified teleportation demonstration suggesting material transport

O.outcome_detail: More accurate mental models of quantum teleportation

cells.quote: For example, educators should highlight that quantum teleportation inherently adheres to the speed of light limit, as its process relies on both a quantum entangled channel and a classical communication channel. Moreover, it is important to understand and connect with the prior knowledge of early learners, but recognize that over-simplification can lead to incorrect mental models [6]. For example, if quantum teleportation is taught with a demonstration in which a person was initially in one place and was transported to another place, it can make students develop a mental model that quantum teleportation is about material (instead of q uantum information) transport from one place to another (although certain aspects of this model such as quantum information vanishing from the original place are correct).
cells.note: This is the authors’ instructional interpretation and recommendation in the discussion, based partly on interviewed educators and cited literature; it is not a tested treatment comparison in this study.

O.outcome_detail: quantum knowledge and skills required for job roles

cells.quote: Among roles requiring no quantum expertise, the sub-themes revolved around business, software development, and hands-on work. At the levels quantum aware and quantum conversant, roles in our sample tend to require an understanding of how an individual’s work fits into the broader scheme of quantum technology and the ability to interface with people at higher levels of quantum expertise. As the level of quantum expertise increases to quantum proficient and quantum expert, so does the degree of specialization of the roles.
cells.note: The study compares qualitatively characterized job roles rather than instructional treatments; the positive direction denotes increasing specialization and quantum requirements across expertise levels.

O.outcome_detail: quantum KSAs required for critical industry tasks

cells.quote: The first category of tasks involves primarily hands-on experimental work. These tasks require advanced lab skills relevant to quantum systems, along with an understanding of the underlying theoretical concepts. ... The final category of tasks require only theoretical knowledge of quantum or QISE.
cells.note: The task categories differ in the type of quantum KSAs required; the text does not establish that one category is better.

O.outcome_detail: balance of theoretical and experimental quantum knowledge

cells.quote: The second category of tasks emphasize theoretical quantum and QISE knowledge. They also require an understanding of experimental techniques and practices, but do not necessarily require the explicit use of experimental skills. The final category of tasks require only theoretical knowledge of quantum or QISE.
cells.note: This is a qualitative contrast in required KSA profiles, not an outcome comparison with a measured effect.

D.treatment: independent projects on QISE applications to societal or medical challenges

O.outcome_detail: understanding of quantum technologies, applications, advantages, and limitations

cells.quote: In general, the students went much further in the development of their understanding of the technologies with much less direct guidance than they likely would have with a very directed class activity.
cells.note: The comparison is the authors' likely counterfactual rather than a concurrently observed control condition.

D.treatment: ethical discussion supported by relevant readings and extended discussion opportunities
D.comparison: little direct ethics instruction and brief discussion

O.outcome_detail: depth and nuance of understanding ethical issues in QISE applications

cells.quote: However, the discussions in Spring 2025 were deeper and more nuanced still as these students were provided with more references and spent more time discussing the issues in class.
cells.note: This comparison is across course cohorts and the high-school program, with differences in instructional time and resources.

O.outcome_detail: ability to discuss ethical implications of quantum technologies in medical applications

cells.quote: All of the students in the Ideas course were able to talk more deeply and with more nuance about the ethical issues confronting quantum technologies than the high-school students.
cells.note: This is a qualitative comparison between student populations and associated learning contexts, not a randomized instructional comparison.

D.treatment: simplified QIST vocabulary such as “qubits” and “measurement basis”
D.comparison: traditional physics terminology focused on physical observables and Hermitian operators

O.outcome_detail: perceived interdisciplinary accessibility and unifying communication

cells.quote: Our analysis reveals that the continuous emergence of linguistic evolutions such as “qubits” and “measurement bases”, rather than a focus on measurement of physical observables and their corresponding Hermitian operators, has begun to create a unifying framework that transcends disciplinary boundaries.
cells.note: The finding is based on qualitative interviews with quantum educators; no learning outcome was experimentally measured.

O.outcome_detail: interest in and attraction to QIST

cells.quote: While the educators acknowledged that there are both benefits and drawbacks to hype in this field, they were broadly optimistic about the long-term potential of QIST.
cells.note: The study reports educators' qualitative perspectives rather than a controlled comparison; the entry's claim that hype attracts interest and industry is not stated in the supplied study excerpt as a measured learning outcome.

D.treatment: thematic synthesis of interview descriptions into four experimental-skill categories

O.outcome_detail: experimental skills articulated as learning goals: instrumentation; computation and data analysis; experimental and project design; communication and collaboration

cells.quote: This process resulted in four overarching categories of experimental skills: (1) instrumentation, (2) computation and data analysis, (3) experimental and project design, and (4) communication and collaboration. Within each category, individual skills were articulated in learning goal language to provide specificity to educators wanting to concretely address those skills in their courses.
cells.note: The study reports a qualitative thematic synthesis of 44 interviews and does not test a treatment against a comparison or report an effect direction.

O.outcome_detail: relative emphasis on computation/data analysis and instrumentation skills

cells.quote: "In contrast, software-oriented roles (e.g., quantum software developer, quantum software engineer) draw most strongly on computation & data analysis, with comparatively limited emphasis on instrumentation skills."
cells.note: The study text supplied above is truncated before this role-type comparison; quote reproduced from the wiki entry as instructed.

O.outcome_detail: breadth of experimental-skill categories used

cells.quote: "Bridging roles exhibit the broadest range of experi- mental skills across categories. The one position classi- fied as a bridging role (e.g., system operator) draws on experimental & project design, communication & collab- oration, computation & data analysis, and instrumenta- tion."
cells.note: Quote is from the wiki entry because the corresponding results text is truncated in the supplied study text.

O.outcome_detail: relative reliance on communication and collaboration versus other skill categories

cells.quote: The results section reports the single bridging position (system operator) draws on all four skill categories, while public-facing and business roles rely most on communication and collaboration while needing some familiarity with other categories.
cells.note: Quote is from the wiki entry because the corresponding results text is truncated in the supplied study text.

D.comparison: courses not addressing quantum sensing-related topics

O.outcome_detail: course coverage of quantum sensing-related topics

cells.quote: In a study of 63 quantum information science and engineering (QISE) courses at the postsecondary level, it was found that only 22% addressed quantum sensing-related topics, and none were dedicated courses on quantum sensing
cells.note: The study text reports this as a finding from a prior study; it does not provide that study's design, learner characteristics, duration, or an inferential comparison.

O.outcome_detail: number of categorized QISE courses

cells.quote: "Of the dedicated QISE courses identified across all institutions, 418 of 514 categorized QISE courses focus on quantum computing and information (81 percent); 70 courses cover quantum technology implementation (which subsumes sensing hardware) and all other QISE categories have fewer than 15 courses each."
cells.note: No study text is available; this quote is from the wiki entry. The entry reports the course-category counts and does not describe the catalog analysis design.

O.outcome_detail: number of identified bachelor's-level positions by role type

cells.quote: Position 1-11 are hardware roles, position 12 is a bridging role, positions 13-21 are software roles, and positions 22-24 are public facing and business roles.
cells.note: Descriptive interview-based comparison of role-category counts; no instructional treatment or causal comparison was reported.
